title: Intel 4004, 8080 and the microprocessor revolution
text:
CHAPTER 6. INTEGRATED CIRCUITS AND MICROPROCESSORS
SECTION 6.3. INTEL 4004, 8080 AND THE MICROPROCESSOR REVOLUTION

By 1970 integrated circuits could hold a few thousand transistors. That was enough to put the entire central processing unit of a simple computer on a single chip: a microprocessor. The first commercial microprocessor, the Intel 4004 of 1971, was designed for a calculator. Within a decade its descendants were inside personal computers, cars, industrial controllers and appliances, and computing changed from a scarce institutional resource into something individuals owned. For a mechatronics engineer this is the most directly relevant chapter of computing history: the microcontroller on your robot is a direct descendant of the 4004.

1. The 4004: a calculator chip that became a computer

In 1969 the Japanese calculator company Busicom approached Intel, then a young memory-chip company founded in 1968 by Robert Noyce and Gordon Moore, to make a set of custom chips for a family of printing calculators. Busicom's own engineers, including Masatoshi Shima, had designed a set of about a dozen specialized logic chips.

Intel engineer Marcian "Ted" Hoff proposed a simpler and more general architecture: a small programmable CPU that executed instructions stored in ROM and kept data in RAM, so that different calculator models could be made by changing the program rather than the hardware. Stanley Mazor helped define the instruction set. Busicom accepted this approach. Detailed design and implementation began in April 1970, led by Federico Faggin, a new Intel hire who had developed silicon-gate MOS technology at Fairchild (using polysilicon instead of aluminum for the gate, which made smaller, faster, denser chips possible). Shima worked with Faggin on the logic design. The first fully working 4004s were delivered for Busicom's calculator prototype in early 1971.

The chipset (the MCS-4) consisted of:

  - 4004: the 4-bit CPU;
  - 4001: ROM with an I/O port (program storage);
  - 4002: RAM with an output port (data storage);
  - 4003: shift register for I/O expansion.

Intel negotiated the right to sell the chips to other customers and announced the 4004 publicly in November 1971 (its production start is usually given as November 15, 1971). Key specifications:

    transistors:       about 2,300
    process:           10 micrometer PMOS silicon gate
    data width:        4 bits (one decimal digit in BCD fits in 4 bits)
    clock:             740 kHz
    instructions:      46
    registers:         16 four-bit index registers, a 4-bit accumulator
    program stack:     3 levels of subroutine return addresses, on chip
    speed:             on the order of tens of thousands of instructions per second

By today's standards the 4004 is tiny, but it was a complete general-purpose stored-program processor (Section 4.4) on one chip, roughly comparable in computing power to ENIAC, which had occupied a room and consumed 150 kW.

2. 8008 and 8080: 8 bits

Intel next built the 8008 (April 1972, about 3,500 transistors), an 8-bit processor originally designed for the Computer Terminal Corporation (later Datapoint), which ultimately did not use it. It was slow and awkward to interface but showed demand for 8-bit processors.

The Intel 8080 (April 1974), designed by Faggin and Shima with others, was a major improvement:

    data width:     8 bits
    address bus:    16 bits (64 kilobytes of addressable memory)
    clock:          2 MHz (later versions faster)
    transistors:    about 4,500 to 6,000 depending on how they are counted
    process:        NMOS, faster than the earlier PMOS

It was fast enough and easy enough to use to serve as the CPU of a general-purpose computer, and it did.

3. A microprocessor from the inside

What does a CPU like the 8080 contain? The same blocks as the stored-program computers of Section 4.4, now on one chip:

  - Registers: a small set of fast storage locations. The 8080 had an 8-bit accumulator A, six 8-bit general registers (B, C, D, E, H, L, usable as 16-bit pairs), a 16-bit stack pointer and a 16-bit program counter, plus a flags register (zero, sign, carry, parity, auxiliary carry).
  - ALU: an arithmetic logic unit built from adders and logic gates (Section 2.2), performing add, subtract, AND, OR, XOR, compare, increment, rotate.
  - Instruction decoder and control: logic (sometimes microcoded) that turns each instruction's bits into control signals sequencing the data path.
  - Bus interface: drives the address bus and data bus to memory and I/O.

A short 8080 assembly program that adds the bytes in a 10-byte array starting at address 2000 hex and stores the sum at address 3000 hex:

    LXI H, 2000h    ; HL <- address of the array
    MVI B, 10       ; B <- loop counter
    MVI A, 0        ; A <- 0 (running sum)
    LOOP:
    ADD M           ; A <- A + memory[HL]
    INX H           ; HL <- HL + 1
    DCR B           ; B <- B - 1, sets zero flag when B becomes 0
    JNZ LOOP        ; if not zero, jump back
    STA 3000h       ; memory[3000h] <- A
    HLT

(";" starts a comment in assembly.) Every element of the history so far appears in these nine lines: binary addition in the ALU (Chapter 2), a stored program fetched from memory (Section 4.4), a conditional branch that makes the machine general (Sections 1.3 and 3.2), and all of it implemented in MOS transistors (Chapter 5) on a planar IC (Section 6.1). And this loop is also, in miniature, the core of neural network inference: a sum over products. Replace ADD M with a multiply-accumulate and the loop computes a dot product, the operation at the heart of a neuron (Chapter 10).

4. Competition: 6800, 6502, Z80

The 8080's success brought competitors quickly:

  - Motorola 6800 (1974), an 8-bit processor with a clean architecture.
  - MOS Technology 6502 (September 1975), designed by a team including Chuck Peddle and Bill Mensch, who had worked on the 6800. It was introduced at a price of about $25, far below competing processors, at a time when the 8080 and 6800 sold for well over a hundred dollars. The 6502 powered the Apple II, the Commodore PET and 64, the Atari 2600 and 8-bit computers, and the Nintendo Entertainment System (in a variant).
  - Zilog Z80 (July 1976), designed by Federico Faggin and Masatoshi Shima after they left Intel to found Zilog. It ran 8080 software and added more registers and instructions. It was used in many CP/M business computers, the Sinclair ZX Spectrum and countless embedded systems.

5. The personal computer

The Altair 8800 from MITS, an Albuquerque electronics company, appeared on the cover of the January 1975 issue of Popular Electronics. It was a kit computer built around the 8080, with switches and lights on the front panel and very little memory, sold by mail order. Hobbyists bought it in large numbers. Two young programmers, Bill Gates and Paul Allen, wrote a BASIC interpreter for it and founded Microsoft. Steve Wozniak and Steve Jobs's Apple I (1976) and Apple II (1977), the Commodore PET (1977) and Tandy TRS-80 (1977) followed, as did a culture of hobbyist clubs such as the Homebrew Computer Club in Silicon Valley.

Intel's 16-bit 8086 (June 1978, about 29,000 transistors) began the x86 architecture. IBM chose the closely related 8088 (8-bit external bus) for the IBM Personal Computer, announced August 12, 1981. The IBM PC's open architecture and the later "clone" market made x86 the dominant desktop and server architecture, which it remains decades later. Motorola's 68000 (1979), with a 32-bit internal architecture, powered the original Apple Macintosh (1984) and many workstations.

6. Microcontrollers: computers that disappear

For mechatronics, the more important branch is the microcontroller: a CPU, program memory, data memory and I/O peripherals all on one chip, intended to be embedded in a product rather than used as a general computer. Texas Instruments' TMS1000 family (introduced in the mid-1970s) is often cited as the first commercially available microcontroller, used in calculators, toys and appliances. Intel's 8048 (1976) and 8051 (1980) became industry standards; the 8051 architecture is still manufactured in variants today. Later families include Microchip's PIC, Atmel's AVR (used in the original Arduino boards) and the many ARM Cortex-M based microcontrollers that dominate embedded systems today.

A modern microcontroller typically includes:

  - CPU core with interrupt controller;
  - flash memory for program, SRAM for data;
  - timers and PWM generators (for motor control);
  - ADCs and sometimes DACs (for sensors and actuators);
  - serial interfaces: UART, SPI, I2C, CAN, USB;
  - general-purpose I/O pins;
  - often, hardware for digital signal processing, and in recent parts, small neural network accelerators.

Microcontrollers made the "mechatronics" field possible: once a programmable computer cost a few dollars, control logic that had required relays (Section 2.1), cams or analog circuits could be implemented in software, making machines smarter, more flexible and cheaper. Today a car contains dozens of microcontrollers, and even simple appliances contain several.

The latest twist connects microcontrollers to the AI story: "TinyML" runs small neural networks for keyword spotting, gesture recognition or anomaly detection on microcontrollers drawing milliwatts, often with specialized instructions for 8-bit multiply-accumulate.

7. The economic effect

The microprocessor changed the economics of computation:

  - Cost per computation fell by orders of magnitude, then kept falling with Moore's law (Section 6.2).
  - Computing moved from centralized mainframes and minicomputers to personal and embedded machines.
  - The mass market for personal computers, and later video game consoles, created the high-volume demand that funded advanced chip manufacturing.

That last point matters for AI. The graphics processors that eventually trained deep neural networks (Chapter 15) were developed for the consumer video game market. Without a mass market for personal computing and gaming, the parallel hardware that enabled the deep learning revolution of the 2010s would not have existed at the scale or price it did.

8. Microprocessors and AI research

  - In the 1970s and early 1980s, serious AI research ran on minicomputers and mainframes (DEC PDP-10s were especially popular in AI labs) or on special-purpose "Lisp machines" (Section 9.2, Chapter 11).
  - By the late 1980s, general-purpose microprocessor workstations (for example from Sun Microsystems) had become fast enough to run Lisp and Prolog well and were far cheaper. This contributed to the collapse of the Lisp machine market, one of the factors of the second AI winter (Section 11.2).
  - In the 1990s and 2000s, statistical machine learning (Chapter 14) ran on commodity x86 PCs and clusters.
  - From the late 2000s, the GPU, another kind of microprocessor, took over the heavy computation of neural networks.

The lesson repeats through the history: mass-market general-purpose hardware tends to overtake expensive special-purpose hardware unless the specialized design offers an overwhelming advantage. GPUs for neural networks are a case where specialization (for graphics, then for matrix math) did win, and they too rode a mass market.

9. Summary

  - The Intel 4004 (production start November 15, 1971), conceived by Ted Hoff with Stanley Mazor and designed by Federico Faggin with Masatoshi Shima for Busicom calculators, was the first commercial single-chip CPU: 4-bit, about 2,300 transistors, 10 micrometer PMOS silicon gate, 740 kHz.
  - The 8008 (1972) and 8080 (1974, 8-bit, 2 MHz, 64 KB address space) made 8-bit microcomputers practical.
  - Competitors included the Motorola 6800, the low-cost MOS 6502 (1975) and the Zilog Z80 (1976).
  - The Altair 8800 (January 1975 Popular Electronics cover) launched personal computing; the 8086 (1978) began x86, and the IBM PC (August 12, 1981) used the 8088.
  - Microcontrollers put CPU, memory and I/O on one chip and made modern mechatronics possible; they now even run small neural networks.
  - The mass consumer market for computers and games funded the hardware, especially GPUs, on which modern AI was built.
